A view of the main street at Bagdad near which city desperate fighting is taking place between the British and the Turkis. The building at the extreme left of the picture is the army head-quarters. In the furthest background (building with star and crescent above it) are the police headquarters, and at the right are the government and municipality buildings. Official Turkish reports tell a bloody repulse of the large British forces attacking the city. 12/3/15

144637 - The mound of Babel upon which was reared the mighty tower of the same name. It now rises majestically from a desolate plain with nothing to suggest the former glory that it helped to bring to Nebuchadnezzar, who twice conquered Jerusalem and made his power felt through out the ancient world.

An immense canal being built by Sir John Jackson, Ltd., contractors and engineers of London, some sixty miles above Babylon do diverge a part of the water of the Euphrates for irrigation purposes. When this undertaking is carried out the banks of the lower Euphrates will once again be dotted with fertility of by-gone days.

THE FALL OF BAGDAD
Our Photo Shows a general view of Bagged

149733 From Bagdad after crossing the narrow neck of thirty miles of the plain of El-Jezirsh that lies between the two great rivers, one arrives at Kalat Falluja in order to cross the Suprates by this bridge of boats and then turn northward on to Alppo, a journey of sixteen to eighteen days by carriage over the most insecure and hard road imaginable. The bridge is so fragile that the horses must be led and carriage pulled across by men for fear the combined weight of carrigas and horses might break through and fall into the river. On the other side of the river stands a typical residence of a wealthy land-owner in Southern Mesopotamia.
